description: The vendor pin (D13). Every third-party browser asset this product serves is
committed under internal/web/static/vendor/ and listed here with a digest,
so `make vendor` re-fetches and verifies and `make vendor-check` re-hashes the
committed bytes and fails on a mismatch.
Why committed at all rather than fetched at boot or bundled through a CDN: the
assets route is campaign-scoped and reader-authorised (S-8), a CDN is a second
origin this product would have to authenticate a player to, and a build that
reaches the network is a build whose output depends on a third party being up.
The cost is a committed blob and a vendor-check that has to actually run.
`origin: "npm"` means `make vendor` fetches the tarball at `source.url`, verifies
it against `source.integrity`, and extracts the member at `files[].inPackage`.
`origin: "local"` is a file this repository wrote: it is committed and hashed
like any other, but there is nothing upstream to re-fetch it from. There is
exactly one local entry and it is the licence, because MIT requires the notice
to travel with the code.
**`source.kind` names the upstream, and there are two.** `npm` is a registry
tarball; `archive` is a project's own release tarball for a tag. Both take the
same path in `tools/vendor`: an `https` URL, a Subresource Integrity digest that
is checked *before* anything is decompressed, and one named member walked out of
the archive. So the label is bookkeeping rather than behaviour — but the
alternative was one label that was wrong for half the entries, in the one file
whose entire job is being trustworthy about provenance. `files[].origin` says
`archive` for a file extracted from the pinned source archive, whatever kind of
upstream served it, and `local` for a file this repository wrote.
The digests are sha256 of the committed bytes, which is what `make vendor-check`
recomputes. They are not the integrity value: that one covers the tarball, which is
never committed, so comparing against it would be checking a file the gate cannot
see.

packages.name: pixi.js
why: PixiJS is the renderer for the live tabletop. It is a WebGL/WebGPU retained-
mode engine, which is the right shape for a map that holds a few hundred
sprites and repaints on a state change rather than on a frame loop:
architecture §15 step 10 chose it and §10.6 records that the client surface
is deliberately limited to placements, fog and initiative, so a new gameplay
system adds no client work.
The `browserAll` entry point is vendored rather than the default one: it is
the build that eagerly initialises the asset and text extensions, which is
what a map needs, and it is the same file the package's own `browser`
condition exports.
Not vendored: pixi.mjs (the unminified twin, 2.2MB), the source maps (the
committed file ends in a sourceMappingURL comment pointing at a file this
repository does not ship — a devtools 404 on purpose, because a 2.2MB map
for an 841KB module is not a cost a self-hosted instance should carry), and
every optional extension (gif, html-source, advanced blend modes, the WebGPU
and WebGPU-adjacent texture loaders), none of which a map renders with.

packages.name: @starfederation/datastar
why: Datastar is the client that consumes this product's `datastar-patch-elements`
frames. UI §7.5's resolution table says the sidebar's fragments are "patched
by Datastar" and architecture §3.1 says templ and Datastar are complements
rather than rivals — templ renders, Datastar places what was rendered — so the
module is what makes §7.5's second column true rather than aspirational.
**The version, and the reason it is 1.0.4 and not the npm `latest`.** The npm
package `@starfederation/datastar` stops at 1.0.0-beta.11 (2025-03-30) and every
release from 0.20.0 onwards renamed the event this product emits: beta.11's
engine/consts declares `datastar-merge-fragments` and greps for
`patch-elements` in that tree return nothing. Datastar's own releases moved to
`datastar-patch-elements` at 1.0.0, and 1.0.4 is the newest (2026-09-21). So the
newest *published* build is the wrong one for this product and pinning it would
have meant a sidebar that never updates — measured, not read off a changelog:
the two spellings were pushed through a real Chromium against both builds and
only the 1.0.4 build acted on the frames this product writes.
`bundles/datastar.js` is vendored rather than `bundles/datastar-core.js` or
`bundles/datastar-rocket.js`. **Core is too small to do this job**: it is the
engine and the signal layer only, and it registers no watcher at all — grepping
the committed bytes for `patch-elements` finds one occurrence in the full bundle
and none in core, because the `datastar-patch-elements` watcher is what
applies a fragment and core does not carry it. Rocket is the Pro bundle, 65KB
against this one's 33KB, and nothing in semiplane's surface is a Pro feature.
Not vendored: the source maps (the committed file carries no sourceMappingURL,
so there is no devtools 404 to accept — this is a distribution build, not a
bundler output), the `.d.ts` files and the `library/src` tree (the type
declarations describe a package this repository does not depend on), and every
other bundle in the same directory.
**The extension is `.js` and not `.mjs`, and it is not an accident.** The file
is an ES module, but `.mjs` would put it into `internal/web`'s existing
`.mjs` audit, which requires every vendored module to carry its own upstream
version banner in the shape `PixiJS - v<version>` — a rule written for one
package. Datastar's banner is `// Datastar v1.0.4`, so the assertion would fail
on a correct artefact. `.js` plus an explicit `mediaType` of
`text/javascript; charset=utf-8` is accurate: the module-ness comes from
`type="module"` on the script element, not from the file name, and the served
media type is what a browser checks.
